topic: Seeing Math: The Geometric Soul of Linear Algebra
target_audience: Undergraduate students and advanced high school students

outline.topic: Seeing Math: The Geometric Soul of Linear Algebra
outline.target_audience: Undergraduate students and advanced high school students

sections.title: Vectors: Movement, Not Just Numbers
sections.content: Introduce the prerequisite concept of a vector. Instead of viewing it as a list of numbers, we visualize it as an arrow in space starting from the origin. This section establishes that 'direction' and 'magnitude' are the fundamental physical properties of vectors.
sections.example: Visualize a small drone at the origin (0,0). To reach a target, it must fly 3 units East and 2 units North. The resulting arrow is the vector [3, 2]. We see the arrow stretch and rotate as the numbers change.

sections.title: Basis Vectors: The DNA of the Grid
sections.content: Explain that every point in the 2D plane is built from two 'basis vectors': i-hat (1,0) and j-hat (0,1). These are the fundamental units of our coordinate system. Every vector is simply a 'scaling and adding' of these two.
sections.example: Imagine a character on a tiled floor. The i-hat vector is one tile to the right; the j-hat vector is one tile up. To get to position (4,3), the character takes 4 steps of i-hat and 3 steps of j-hat.

sections.title: Matrices as Space Morphing
sections.content: Shift from static vectors to dynamic transformations. A matrix is not just a box of numbers; it is a 'function' that moves space. Key rule: The columns of a matrix tell us exactly where i-hat and j-hat land after the transformation. The rest of the grid follows linearly.
sections.example: Take a 2x2 matrix where the first column is [0, 1] and the second is [-1, 0]. Watch as the entire grid rotates 90 degrees counter-clockwise because i-hat moved to where j-hat used to be, and j-hat moved to (-1,0).

sections.title: The Determinant: The Scaling Factor
sections.content: Define the determinant geometrically. It represents the factor by which areas are scaled during a transformation. If the determinant is 2, the area doubles. If it is 0, the space is 'squished' into a lower dimension (like a line or a point).
sections.example: A rubber sheet has a drawing of a circle with an area of 1 square inch. After applying a matrix transformation with a determinant of 3, the circle stretches into an ellipse with an area of 3 square inches.

sections.title: Application: Computer Graphics & Animation
sections.content: Conclude by showing how these geometric intuitions are the backbone of modern technology. Matrix transformations allow us to rotate, scale, and project 3D objects onto 2D screens in real-time.
sections.example: Show a 3D model of a mechanical cat. To make the cat 'run,' the computer applies different matrices to the vectors defining its limbs, rotating and translating them hundreds of times per second.

storyboard.title: Vectors: Movement, Not Just Numbers
lecture_lines: A vector is more than just a list of numbers.
Imagine it as an arrow pointing in a direction.
This arrow represents a specific movement through space.
Its length, or magnitude, shows the distance moved.
Watch the arrow stretch as its values increase.
animations: Draw a white coordinate grid (labels: X-axis #FFFFFF, Y-axis #FFFFFF). Animate a green (#00FF00) arrow (vector) starting at (0,0) and pointing to (2,1). Label it 'Vector'.
Flash the arrow's length (magnitude) and tip (direction) in yellow (#FFFF00).
Clear previous vector. Animate a small blue (#0000FF) square (drone) moving from (0,0) to (3,2) following a dashed light gray (#A9A9A9) line.
Create a bold white (#FFFFFF) vector arrow from (0,0) to (3,2). Display text '[3, 2]' next to the tip in white (#FFFFFF).
Scale the [3, 2] vector by 1.5x, making it longer while keeping the same direction. Change color to orange (#FFA500) during scaling.

storyboard.title: Basis Vectors: The DNA of the Grid
lecture_lines: Every vector starts from two fundamental units.
i-hat points one unit to the right.
j-hat points one unit straight up.
Any point is reached by scaling and adding these two.
They are the building blocks of our entire coordinate system.
animations: Show a grid. Animate a red arrow (#FF0000) from (0,0) to (1,0) labeled 'i-hat' and a green arrow (#00FF00) from (0,0) to (0,1) labeled 'j-hat'.
Highlight i-hat and j-hat by flashing them.

Animate the creation of vector (4,3) by showing 4 red i-hat arrows placed tip-to-tail horizontally, followed by 3 green j-hat arrows placed tip-to-tail vertically. Draw a white (#FFFFFF) vector from (0,0) to (4,3).

storyboard.title: Matrices as Space Morphing
lecture_lines: A matrix is a function that transforms space.
It moves the entire grid in a linear way.
The columns tell us where basis vectors land.
See i-hat and j-hat move to their new positions.
The rest of the grid follows their lead perfectly.
animations: Display a white grid with i-hat (red #FF0000) and j-hat (green #00FF00).
Show a 2x2 matrix text: [[0, -1], [1, 0]] in white (#FFFFFF). Highlight the first column [0, 1] in yellow (#FFFF00).
Highlight the second column [-1, 0] in yellow (#FFFF00). Animate j-hat rotating from (0,1) to (-1,0).
Morph the entire white grid background to rotate 90 degrees counter-clockwise along with the vectors.

storyboard.title: The Determinant: The Scaling Factor
lecture_lines: The determinant measures how much areas scale during transformation.
A determinant of two means the area has doubled.
If it is zero, the space squishes into a line.
animations: Show a unit square defined by i-hat and j-hat. Fill it with a light blue (#ADD8E6) color. Label area '1'.
Scale the square by 2x horizontally. The area stretches. Change the fill color to dark blue (#00008B) and update label to 'Area = 2'. Show text 'Det = 2' in white (#FFFFFF).
Flatten the square into a single flat line on the x-axis. Change color to red (#FF0000). Show text 'Det = 0' and label 'Area = 0'.

storyboard.title: Application: Computer Graphics & Animation
lecture_lines: These geometric transformations power modern computer graphics.
Matrices rotate and scale 3D models in real-time.
Linear algebra brings digital worlds to life through movement.
animations: Display a simple stick-figure or 'mechanical cat' (simple polygon shape) in light gray (#D3D3D3).
Apply a rotation matrix to the shape, making it spin. Then apply a scaling matrix to make it 'jump' (stretch vertically). Highlight the changing matrix values in gold (#FFD700).
Show a grid of many such shapes all transforming simultaneously to represent a complex scene.
